title: It moved to the right
objective: Recognize appendicitis by right lower quadrant or periumbilical pain, and report it because perforation can cause peritonitis and sepsis

sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-PN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Coordinated Care includes care within the legal scope of practice; Physiological Adaptation includes recognizing and reporting a change in the client's condition.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

brief.situation: 14:00 in a family medicine clinic. You are the LPN rooming patients. Ms. Hale, 19, walked in without an appointment with belly pain since last night. The provider is with another patient for the next 20 minutes.
handover: Her mother drove her and says, 'It's probably something she ate.'

Clinic policy: the LPN takes vital signs and a focused history and reports any abnormal finding or urgent concern to the provider at once, interrupting if needed; the LPN does not send a walk-in home without the provider seeing them.
Standing order: the LPN may give acetaminophen for fever under 38.5 C only after the provider has seen the patient.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what her findings mean, what not to do, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What do Ms. Hale's findings suggest, why is it urgent, and what do you do within your role?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Possible appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea, fever and a raised pulse, pain on coughing and right-sided pain when the left is pressed; it can perforate and cause peritonitis and sepsis, with risk rising after 36 hours.
parts.modelAnswer: Her pain started around her navel and moved to the right lower belly, she has no appetite, she's nauseated and febrile, and pressing on the left hurts on the right. That sounds like appendicitis. It can perforate and cause peritonitis and sepsis, so it can't wait.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Reports to the provider at once, interrupting; keeps her nothing by mouth; does not give medication outside the standing order or mask the symptoms; does not send her home; documents.
parts.modelAnswer: Interrupt the provider now, keep her nothing by mouth, and don't give her anything that would mask the pain or that I'm not allowed to give yet. She doesn't go home until the provider has seen her. Document what I found.

perforated.headline: Perforation
perforated.body: Periumbilical pain that moves to the right lower quadrant with anorexia, nausea and fever is appendicitis until proved otherwise. Report it at once; perforation causes peritonitis and sepsis.

referred.headline: Referred in time
referred.body: You took a focused history and vital signs, recognized the pattern, kept her nothing by mouth, didn't mask it, and interrupted the provider within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pain that began around the navel and moved to the right lower quadrant, with anorexia, nausea, a temperature over 38, a raised pulse, pain on coughing and right-sided pain when the left lower quadrant is pressed, suggests appendicitis. It can perforate, causing peritonitis and sepsis, with risk rising beyond about 36 hours of symptoms. Within the LPN role: take vital signs and a focused history, keep her nothing by mouth, give nothing outside the standing order, never send her home unseen, and interrupt the provider at once. Then document.

perfQ.ask: As she leaves: which change would suggest the appendix has ruptured?

choices.label: A rigid, board-like abdomen with guarding, fever and a rising pulse

perfQ.explain: Alert the provider to peritonitis, a board-like abdomen with rigidity and guarding, which can indicate a ruptured appendix; and to tachycardia or fever.
